items.question_text:
The position-time (x–t) graph of an object moving in one dimension consists of straight-line segments passing through the points (0 s, 0 m), (2.5 s, 50 m), (7.5 s, 50 m), (10.0 s, 100 m), and (15.0 s, 0 m). Using this information, calculate:
(a) the average velocity over the time interval from 0 to 10 s
(b) the instantaneous velocity at the time instants t = 2 s, t = 5 s, t = 8 s, and t = 12 s
items.figure_description: A graph of position x (in m) plotted against time t (in s). The curve starts at (0, 0), rises with a constant positive slope to (2.5, 50), stays horizontal at x = 50 until t = 7.5, continues upward linearly to (10.0, 100), and then descends linearly to meet the time axis at (15.0, 0).

solution.approach: Find the average velocity from the net displacement over 0 to 10 s, then read the slope of the graph at each given time for the instantaneous velocities.

steps.text: Average velocity is the net displacement divided by the time interval, from t = 0 to t = 10 s.
At t = 2 s the particle is on the rising segment from (0,0) to (2.5,50); its slope is the velocity.
At t = 5 s the particle is on the flat segment from t = 2.5 s to t = 7.5 s, where x stays at 50 m.
At t = 8 s the particle is on the segment rising from (7.5,50) to (10,100); its slope is the velocity.
At t = 12 s the particle is on the falling segment from (10,100) to (15,0); its slope is the velocity.

common_mistakes.text: Carrying the slope from the first rising segment forward and reporting v(5) = 20 m/s, without noticing the graph is flat between t = 2.5 s and t = 7.5 s.
Reporting the speed 20 m/s at t = 12 s without the negative sign that shows the particle is moving back towards the origin.

items.question_text: An elevator begins moving upward from a stationary state, with its acceleration changing over time as shown in the given graph. The acceleration is 2 ms⁻² between t = 0 and t = 4 s, remains 0 from t = 4 s to t = 8 s, and is −2 ms⁻² between t = 8 s and t = 12 s. Determine the total vertical displacement of the elevator from its initial level by the time it stops.
items.figure_description: An acceleration-time graph showing acceleration a in ms⁻² on the vertical axis and time t in s on the horizontal axis. A horizontal line segment extends from t = 0 to t = 4 s at a = 2 ms⁻². The curve lies on the time axis (a = 0) from t = 4 s to t = 8 s. A horizontal line segment extends from t = 8 s to t = 12 s at a = −2 ms⁻².

solution.approach: Read the acceleration in each of the three time segments, find the velocity at each segment boundary, and add the distance covered in each segment.

steps.text: From t = 0 to 4 s, acceleration is 2 ms⁻² from rest. Find the velocity and distance covered by the end of this segment.
From t = 4 to 8 s, acceleration is 0, so the lift moves at the constant velocity 8 ms⁻¹. Find the distance covered.
From t = 8 to 12 s, acceleration is −2 ms⁻². Check that the lift comes to rest exactly at t = 12 s.
Find the distance covered while the velocity falls from 8 ms⁻¹ to 0 over this last segment.
Add the three distances to get the total height above the starting point.

common_mistakes.text: Treating zero acceleration in the middle segment as zero velocity, so skipping the 32 m travelled at constant speed and adding only the first and last segments: 16 + 16 = 32 m.

items.question_text: An object possesses an initial velocity v₀ = 10 ms⁻¹ and is subjected to a deceleration of magnitude 0.2v², where v represents its instantaneous velocity. What will be the velocity of the object at t = 2 s?

solution.approach: Write the retardation as dv/dt = −0.2v² and separate the variables to find v as a function of t.

steps.text: Write the equation of motion using the given retardation.
Separate the variables and integrate from v₀ = 10 at t = 0 to v at time t.
Rearrange to express 1/v.
Substitute v₀ = 10 and t = 2 s.
Take the reciprocal to find the velocity after 2 s.

items.question_text:
A particle travels along a straight horizontal line with its velocity expressed as v = (3t² − 6t) m/s, where t is the time in seconds. Starting from the origin at t = 0, calculate the following for the duration between t = 0 and t = 3.5 s:
(a) The total distance covered by the particle
(b) The average velocity of the particle
(c) The average speed of the particle

solution.approach: Split the motion where velocity reverses sign, integrate to get position, add distances in each part for total distance, and use net displacement for average velocity.

steps.text: Set v = 3t² − 6t equal to zero to find when the particle reverses direction.
Integrate v with respect to t, taking the particle at the origin at t = 0, to get its position.
Find the position at t = 0, t = 2 s and t = 3.5 s.
From t = 0 to t = 2 s the particle moves from 0 to −4 m; from t = 2 s to t = 3.5 s it moves from −4 m to 6.125 m. Add these distances.
steps.why_this_step: Total distance adds the length travelled in each leg of the trip, even where the particle doubles back.

steps.text: Average velocity uses net displacement over the interval; average speed uses total distance over the interval.
steps.equation: average velocity = 6.125/3.5 = 1.75 m/s, average speed = 14.125/3.5 ≈ 4.04 m/s

final_answer.value: distance travelled = 14.125 m, average velocity = 1.75 m/s, average speed ≈ 4.04 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Taking the net displacement x(3.5) − x(0) = 6.125 m as the total distance, missing that the particle reverses direction at t = 2 s and travels back and forth.
Reporting average speed as equal to average velocity, 1.75 m/s, without separating distance from displacement.

concept_tags: velocity as a function of time

items.question_text:
An object travels along a circular path having a radius of 4 cm at a uniform speed of 1 cm/s. Determine:
(a) The time period of revolution for the object.
(b) The magnitudes of the average speed, average velocity, and average acceleration over the duration from t = 0 to t = T/4, where T denotes the time period.

solution.approach: Use circumference over speed for the period, then work out the distance, the chord, and the velocity change over a quarter turn.

steps.text: The time period is the circumference divided by the constant speed.
From t = 0 to t = T/4 the particle covers a quarter of the circle, in a time of T/4.
Since the speed never changes, the average speed over any interval equals this constant speed.
The displacement is the straight chord joining the start and end points, which are 90° apart on the circle, so the average velocity is this chord divided by the time.
steps.equation: displacement = r√2 = 4√2 cm, average velocity = 4√2/(2π) ≈ 0.90 cm/s

steps.text: Over the quarter turn the velocity direction rotates by 90° while its magnitude stays at 1 cm/s, giving a velocity-vector change of v√2; the average acceleration is this change divided by the time.
steps.why_this_step: The velocity vectors at the two instants are perpendicular, so their difference has magnitude v√2, not zero.

final_answer.value: (a) T = 8π s ≈ 25.13 s. (b) average speed = 1 cm/s, average velocity ≈ 0.90 cm/s, average acceleration ≈ 0.23 cm/s²

common_mistakes.text: Subtracting the two speed values instead of the velocity vectors, 1 − 1 = 0, and concluding the average acceleration is zero, which ignores the change in direction.
Using the quarter-circle arc length as the displacement instead of the straight chord, which gives an average velocity equal to the average speed, 1 cm/s.

items.question_text: A particle travels along a straight path such that its speed v decreases as a linear function of position s, starting at 20 m/s when s = 0 and reaching zero at s = 30 m. Find the acceleration of the body at the position s = 15 m.

solution.approach: Write velocity as a linear function of displacement, then use a = v(dv/ds) at s = 15 m.

steps.text: Velocity falls linearly from 20 m/s at s = 0 to 0 at s = 30 m; write v as a function of s.
Differentiate v with respect to s; the slope is constant.
Find v at s = 15 m.
Use a = v(dv/ds) with v = 10 m/s and dv/ds = −2/3 to find the acceleration.

common_mistakes.text: Using the starting velocity 20 m/s instead of the velocity at s = 15 m, giving a = 20 × (−2/3) = −13.3 m/s².
Dropping the negative sign on the slope and writing a = 10 × (2/3) = 6.67 m/s².

items.question_text: A particle, initially at rest, begins rectilinear motion with a uniform acceleration. When a duration t₀ has elapsed, the direction of this acceleration is reversed while its magnitude remains unchanged. Find the total elapsed time T from the start until the particle arrives back at its starting point.

solution.approach: Split the motion into the first phase of duration t₀ and a second phase with reversed acceleration, then find when the total displacement returns to zero.

steps.text: In the first phase, from rest with acceleration a for time t₀, find the velocity and displacement reached.
In the second phase the acceleration becomes −a. Let τ be the time measured after t₀, and write the total displacement at that point.
Set the total displacement to zero and solve the resulting quadratic for τ.
steps.equation: ½t₀² + t₀τ − ½τ² = 0 → τ² − 2t₀τ − t₀² = 0 → τ = t₀(1 + √2)

steps.text: Add τ to t₀ for the total time T at which the point mass is back at the start.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the second phase exactly mirrors the first and the point mass returns at T = 2t₀ ignores that the mass keeps moving forward for a while in the second phase before it turns back.

items.question_text: At the same instant, two bodies, A and B, travel along a straight path in an identical direction. Particle A has an initial speed of 3 m/s and maintains a constant acceleration of 1 m/s², while particle B has an initial speed of 1 m/s and an acceleration of 2 m/s². If particle A begins at a position 10 m behind particle B, determine the closest distance of approach between the two particles.

solution.approach: Write the separation between B and A as a function of time and minimize it with calculus.

steps.text: Write each particle's position from its own start, then the separation as B's position minus A's position, starting from the given 10 m gap.
Set the derivative of the separation to zero to find the time of closest approach.
Substitute t = 2 s back into the separation to get the minimum distance.
steps.why_this_step: The second derivative of s(t) is positive, so this turning point is a minimum, not a maximum.

common_mistakes.text: Using only the initial speeds, 3 m/s and 1 m/s, and ignoring the accelerations suggests the gap keeps closing forever, missing that B's larger acceleration later pulls it ahead again.

items.question_text:
From a height of 12 m, a ball is projected straight up with an initial speed of 18 m/s. Exactly at this moment, an open-platform lift crosses the 5 m mark while ascending at a steady speed of 2 m/s. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², calculate:
(a) the time and location where the ball encounters the platform,
(b) the velocity of the ball measured relative to the platform upon collision.

solution.approach: Write the ball's height under gravity and the elevator's height at constant speed as functions of time, set them equal to find when they meet, then find their relative velocity.

steps.text: Write the ball's height using free-fall kinematics and the elevator's height using constant velocity.
Set the two heights equal and simplify to a quadratic in t.
Solve the quadratic and keep the positive root.
Find the meeting height using the elevator's equation.
Find the relative velocity of the ball with respect to the elevator at this instant.

final_answer.value: (a) the ball meets the elevator at t ≈ 3.66 s, at a height of about 12.31 m. (b) relative velocity of the ball with respect to the elevator ≈ 19.83 m/s, directed downward.

common_mistakes.text: Solving for when the ball returns to the elevator's starting height of 5 m, ignoring that the elevator itself keeps moving up, which gives the wrong time t ≈ 4.03 s.
Assuming the ball is still moving upward at the meeting instant instead of already falling, giving a wrong relative velocity of about 15.83 m/s instead of 19.83 m/s.

items.question_text:
Given below are two statements labeled as Assertion and Reason. Choose the appropriate option that describes them.

Assertion: Based on the formula a = v(dv/ds), whenever the velocity of a body equals zero, its acceleration must likewise vanish.
Reason: The quantity a defined in this expression represents the instantaneous acceleration.

options.label: a
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

options.label: b
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

options.label: c
options.text: Assertion is true, but Reason is false.

options.label: d
options.text: Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

solution.approach: Test the claim with free fall from rest: at the starting instant velocity is zero, but the acceleration a = v dv/ds still gives a finite, nonzero value.

steps.text: For free fall from rest through a height s, the speed follows v² = 2gs, so v = √(2gs) and dv/ds = g/v.
Form the product a = v dv/ds; the v in front cancels the v in the denominator of dv/ds, leaving a constant, even as v approaches zero near the start.
steps.why_this_step: As s becomes very small, v also becomes very small, but dv/ds grows without bound, so the product v dv/ds stays finite and equal to g rather than going to zero.

steps.text: This shows a = v dv/ds does not force acceleration to zero when velocity is zero; the Assertion's conclusion is false, while the Reason, that a in this formula is the instantaneous acceleration, is a true definition on its own and does not justify the false conclusion.

final_answer.value: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Substituting v = 0 directly into a = v dv/ds and reading off a = 0, without checking that dv/ds can be infinite at that point.

items.question_text:
A particle travels within the x-y plane such that its position coordinates at instant t are given by (2t, t²). Determine:
(a) the equation of the particle's trajectory,
(b) its velocity at time t, and
(c) its acceleration at any instant t.

solution.approach: Eliminate t between the two coordinates to get the path, then differentiate each coordinate once for velocity and again for acceleration.

steps.text: The coordinates are x = 2t and y = t². Solve the first for t and substitute into the second.
This is the equation of the path traced by the particle.
Differentiate x and y with respect to t to get the velocity components.
steps.equation: vₓ = dx/dt = 2 ms⁻¹, v_y = dy/dt = 2t ms⁻¹

steps.text: The velocity vector and its magnitude follow from these components.
Differentiate the velocity components again to get the acceleration.
steps.equation: aₓ = dvₓ/dt = 0, a_y = dv_y/dt = 2 ms⁻², so acceleration is 2 ms⁻² along y, constant for all t

final_answer.value: (a) y = x²/4 (a parabola), (b) velocity has components vₓ = 2 ms⁻¹, v_y = 2t ms⁻¹, magnitude 2√(1+t²) ms⁻¹, (c) acceleration is constant, 2 ms⁻² along y, at every time t

common_mistakes.text: Writing the trajectory as y = t² without eliminating t, which leaves the path expressed in terms of time instead of in terms of x and y.

items.question_text: The position of an object travelling across the xy-plane is given as a function of time by x = 2t² and y = t³, where coordinates x and y are measured in metres and time t is in seconds. Determine the average acceleration of the object over the duration from t = 0 to t = 2 s.

solution.approach: Differentiate the coordinates to get the velocity components, then find the average acceleration from the change in velocity over the time interval.

steps.text: Differentiate x and y with respect to time to get the velocity components.
Evaluate the velocity components at t = 0 and t = 2 s.
steps.equation: at t=0: vₓ=0, v_y=0; at t=2: vₓ=8 m/s, v_y=12 m/s

steps.text: Divide the change in each velocity component by the time interval.
Combine the components as a vector and find the magnitude.

common_mistakes.text: Finding the instantaneous acceleration aₓ=4, a_y=6t at t=2 s instead of averaging, giving (4î + 12ĵ) m/s².

items.question_text: A particle moving in the x-y plane experiences a time-dependent acceleration described by a = (2t î + 3t² ĵ) m/s². At the moment t = 0, it begins moving from the origin with an initial velocity of 2 m/s directed along the positive x-axis. Determine the velocity vector and the position coordinates of the particle at t = 1 s.

solution.approach: Integrate the acceleration once for velocity, adding the initial velocity, then integrate again for position, starting from the origin.

steps.text: Integrate a with respect to time and add the initial velocity to get v(t).
Substitute t = 1 s.
Integrate v with respect to time, starting from the origin, to get the coordinates.
Substitute t = 1 s to get the coordinates.

common_mistakes.text: Integrating the acceleration for velocity without adding the initial velocity of 2 m/s along the x-axis gives v(1) = (î + ĵ) m/s instead of (3î + ĵ) m/s.
Integrating the acceleration components twice without carrying the initial velocity into the position integral gives an x-coordinate of 1/3 m instead of 7/3 m.

items.question_text:
A body is thrown vertically upward with an initial speed of 40 m/s. Taking the upward direction as positive and assuming g = 10 m/s², draw the acceleration-time (a-t), velocity-time (v-t), and displacement-time (s-t) curves representing its entire motion until it returns to the launch level.
(a) Acceleration-time (a-t) graph
(b) Velocity-time (v-t) graph
(c) Displacement-time (s-t) graph
items.figure_description:
Three kinematic graphs from t = 0 s to t = 8 s:
1. a-t graph: A horizontal line at a = −10 m/s² spanning from t = 0 s to t = 8 s.
2. v-t graph: A straight line with a constant negative slope beginning at (0 s, +40 m/s), intersecting the time axis at (4 s, 0 m/s), and ending at (8 s, −40 m/s).
3. s-t graph: An inverted parabola starting at the origin (0 s, 0 m), reaching a peak at (4 s, 80 m), and returning to zero at (8 s, 0 m).

solution.approach: Use the equations of motion under constant gravity with upward positive to find the times, then plot each quantity against time.

steps.text: Find the time to reach the highest point, where velocity becomes zero.
Find the maximum height reached.
Find the total time of flight back to the starting point.
Describe the a-t graph: acceleration stays constant throughout, since gravity does not change.
steps.equation: a = −10 m/s² for the whole interval t = 0 to t = 8 s

steps.text: Describe the v-t graph using v = u + at.
steps.equation: v starts at +40 m/s at t = 0, falls in a straight line, crosses zero at t = 4 s, reaches −40 m/s at t = 8 s

steps.text: Describe the s-t graph using s = ut + ½at², which is symmetric about the highest point.
steps.equation: s rises from 0 to a peak of 80 m at t = 4 s, then falls back to 0 m at t = 8 s

final_answer.value: a-t graph: constant −10 m/s² from t = 0 to t = 8 s. v-t graph: a straight line from +40 m/s at t = 0 to −40 m/s at t = 8 s, crossing zero at t = 4 s. s-t graph: a curve rising from 0 to a peak of 80 m at t = 4 s and returning to 0 m at t = 8 s.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the acceleration as zero at the highest point, since velocity is zero there, confuses velocity with acceleration; gravity acts throughout at −10 m/s².
Using T = u/g = 4 s as the total flight time instead of 2u/g = 8 s stops the graphs halfway, missing the fall back to the ground.

items.question_text: The position of an object traveling along a straight path varies with time according to the relation x = 32t − (8/3)t³, where the coordinate x is in metres and time t is in seconds. Determine its acceleration at the moment it momentarily comes to a stop.

solution.approach: Differentiate the position function to get velocity, find the time the particle is at rest, then differentiate again to get acceleration at that time.

steps.text: Differentiate the position function to get the velocity.
Set the velocity to zero and solve for the physically valid (positive) time.
Differentiate the velocity to get acceleration, then evaluate it at t = 2 s.

common_mistakes.text: Solving 32 − 8t² = 0 and taking the negative root t = −2 s instead of the physical t = 2 s, giving a(−2) = 32 ms⁻².

items.question_text: An object is thrown straight up into the air with a starting speed of 40 m/s. Determine both its total displacement and the overall distance it travels during the first 6 s of its flight. (Use g = 10 m/s²)

solution.approach: Check whether the particle has already turned back within the 6 s, then add the upward and downward distances separately for the distance covered.

steps.text: Displacement in 6 s follows directly from the standard equation of motion, taking upward as positive.
Find the time taken to reach the highest point, where the velocity becomes zero.
Since 4 s is less than 6 s, the particle has already turned around and is falling back for the last 2 s; find the maximum height it reached.
Find how far it falls back down in the remaining time after reaching the top.
The displacement is the height reached minus the distance fallen back, matching the direct calculation, while the total distance covered is the height reached plus the distance fallen back.
steps.why_this_step: Distance keeps adding up regardless of direction, while displacement is the net change in position.

common_mistakes.text: Reporting the distance as equal to the displacement, 60 m, without checking that the particle reversed direction before 6 s had passed.
Assuming the particle has returned all the way to the starting point by 6 s and taking the distance as twice the maximum height, 160 m.
